notes.meaning: The angel of the Lord traveled from Gilgal to Bochim to deliver a solemn message to Israel. He reminded them that He had brought them out of slavery in Egypt into the land promised to their ancestors. He also declared that He would never break His covenant, which was His sacred agreement with them.

God had given Israel clear orders to make no peace pacts with the Canaanites and to tear down their pagan altars. Instead of obeying, the people allowed those false altars to remain standing. God asked what they had done, showing that their disobedience had no good excuse.

Because Israel tolerated the wicked nations, God announced that He would no longer drive them out. These remaining peoples would become like thorns in Israel's sides, bringing constant pain and trouble. Their false gods would serve as a dangerous trap, pulling God's people into sin.

When the angel delivered this message, the whole assembly of Israel began to weep loudly. They felt sharp grief and fear over the painful troubles that were coming. Sadly, their weeping was only a burst of emotion rather than a lasting change of heart.

The people named the place Bochim, which means "weepers," because of their loud crying. They also offered animal sacrifices there to seek God's mercy and forgiveness. Tears alone could not take away their wrongdoing, so they turned to the altar of the Lord.

The story looks back to the moment when Joshua sent all the tribes out across the land. Every family went to settle their own inherited piece of ground. This background explains how the nation drifted into trouble after their initial settlement.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many critical scholars view this verse as the start of an editorial framework composed during or after the exile to link the stories of the judges with Joshua.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Traditional Catholic commentary sees this passage as opening the book's main theme, showing that when Israel leaves God, God leaves them for a time until they repent.

notes.meaning: The people remained faithful to the Lord as long as Joshua and the older leaders lived. These elders had personally seen the miraculous things God did when He gave Israel the land. Remembering God's mighty deeds helped that first generation stay loyal to Him.

Joshua died at the age of one hundred and ten after a long life of leadership. Scripture honors him with the noble title "the servant of the LORD." His death marked the close of a faithful era for the nation.

Israel buried Joshua on his own family land at Timnath-heres in the hill country of Ephraim. The gravesite lay north of Mount Gaash. The nation honored him with this resting place in recognition of his faithful service.

Eventually, that entire older generation died and was buried. A new generation grew up who had not personally witnessed the great works God had done for Israel. Without their own personal faith in the Lord, they quickly drifted into spiritual darkness.

The younger Israelites did what was evil in the eyes of the Lord by worshipping the Baals. Baal was the general name for the local false gods worshipped throughout Canaan. By turning to these idols, the people openly rebelled against the true God.

The people abandoned the Lord, the very God who had rescued their ancestors from slavery in Egypt. They adopted the religious practices of the surrounding nations and bowed down to man-made idols. This unfaithfulness provoked the Lord's holy anger.

Israel completely turned away from the Lord to serve Baal and the Ashtoreths. Baal was worshipped as a weather and crop god, while the Ashtoreths were female idols tied to fertility. Trying to serve these idols alongside the Lord was the same as deserting Him altogether.

The Lord's anger burned against Israel, and He handed them over to enemy raiders who robbed them. He sold them into the power of their foes, meaning He left them without divine protection. As a result, the Israelites could no longer stand firm in battle.

Whenever Israel marched out to fight, the Lord worked against them instead of helping them win. This brought severe trouble, just as God had warned in His law if they broke His covenant. The people soon found themselves in terrible misery and distress.

In His great mercy, the Lord raised up leaders known as judges to rescue the people. God gave these leaders special courage and wisdom to defeat the foreign armies that were plundering Israel. Even though the people had sinned, God still provided deliverers to save them.

Even when judges were leading them, Israel refused to listen and keep God's commands. They committed spiritual adultery—being unfaithful to God by worshipping idols—and bowed to false gods. They quickly abandoned the obedient path that their ancestors had faithfully walked.

Whenever the Lord appointed a judge, He was with that leader and rescued Israel as long as the judge lived. God felt deep pity when He heard His people groaning under cruel masters. It was God's tender mercy, not Israel's good behavior, that prompted Him to deliver them.

As soon as a judge died, the people plunged right back into idolatry and became even more corrupt than their parents. They bowed down to false gods and refused to give up their stubborn ways. Each cycle left the nation in worse shape than before.

The Lord burned with anger against Israel because they had broken the holy covenant He had given their ancestors. They chose to ignore His voice and disobey His commands. Because of this rebellion, God announced that their unfaithfulness would bring lasting consequences.

God declared that He would stop driving out the remaining Canaanite nations that were still in the land when Joshua died. Because Israel broke their agreement with God, He withdrew His promise to clear out their enemies. Those foreign nations would now remain in place.

God used these surviving nations to test whether Israel would choose to obey Him. The test would show whether the people would walk in God's ways like their ancestors had done. It revealed their true loyalty and proved how easily their hearts turned toward sin.

The Lord had left these nations in the land rather than letting Joshua wipe them all out at once. Leaving them gave the Israelites time to grow in population and prevented wild animals from taking over the land. It also provided a way for God to test Israel's faith and correct them when they strayed.
